tips.title: Rusting needs air and water
tips.body: **Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.** Remove either one and it does not happen. That is why the classic experiment uses three tubes: one with both, one with the air removed, one with the water removed.

tips.title: Corrosion is the general word
tips.body: **Corrosion** is the **destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment**. **Rusting** is one example of corrosion — the one that happens to **iron and steel**. Aluminium corrodes too, but it does not rust.

tips.title: Barriers keep air and water out
tips.body: **Greasing, painting and electroplating** all work the same way: they put a **physical barrier** between the iron and the air and water. Scratch the barrier and rusting starts there, because the protection was never chemical.

tips.title: Sacrificial means more reactive
tips.body: A **sacrificial** coating contains a **more reactive metal**, so it **corrodes instead of** the iron. **Zinc galvanises iron** because zinc is above iron in the reactivity series. Tin is below iron, so tin plating protects only while it is intact.

tips.title: Aluminium protects itself
tips.body: Aluminium forms an **oxide coating** that **protects the metal from further corrosion**. The layer sticks tightly and seals the surface, which is why aluminium survives outdoors despite being more reactive than iron.

why.matters:
Corrosion is not wear. It is a **chemical reaction** between a material and its surroundings, in which the material is used up — and for iron it needs **both air and water**, which is why the same gate survives in a desert and disintegrates in a field.

Once you know what a reaction needs, you know how to stop it: take one of the reactants away with a barrier, or give the corrosion something it would rather eat. Both defences are in this topic, and only one of them survives a scratch.

examples.title: Why a galvanised nail survives a scratch
examples.body:
Paint a gate and you have a **barrier**: it keeps the air and water off, and it works right up until something chips it. Then the iron rusts at the chip, and the rust flakes off and lets the next layer go.

Galvanising does something better. The zinc is **more reactive than iron**, so it corrodes in the iron's place — and it keeps doing that from wherever it still is, even after the coating is scratched. A galvanised bucket with a dent in it is still protected; a painted one is not.

visual.alt: A table comparing a barrier coating such as paint, which keeps air and water out but fails where it is scratched, with galvanising, where the zinc is above iron in the reactivity series and corrodes in its place even when scratched

examples.title: Why rust falls off and aluminium oxide does not
examples.body:
Aluminium is **more reactive** than iron, so it should corrode faster — and it does, immediately, the moment it meets air. Then it stops.

The difference is what the oxide does next. Aluminium oxide forms a thin, tight layer that **sticks to the surface and seals it**, so the metal underneath never meets the air again. Rust is flaky: it lifts off and exposes fresh iron, which rusts, and lifts off. One metal armours itself; the other eats itself from the outside in.

visual.alt: A flow chart of why rusting never stops: iron with air and water forms rust, the rust flakes off, fresh iron is exposed underneath, and the cycle begins again

examples.title: The three tubes that prove it
examples.body:
The classic experiment is three boiling tubes, each with an iron nail, and each one taking away a single thing. It is the clearest example in the course of testing one variable at a time.

Air **and** water together: the nail rusts. Boiled water with oil on top, so there is no dissolved air: it does not. Dry air over a drying agent: it does not. Neither condition is enough on its own, which is why a barrier only has to exclude **one** of them to work — and why oiling a bike chain is enough.

steps.title: Corrosion and rusting
steps.body:
**Corrosion** is the **destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment**. It is not wear or scratching — it is a **chemical** change, in which the material reacts and is consumed.

**Rusting is an example of corrosion**: the corrosion of **iron and steel**. It is worth being precise, because only iron rusts. Other metals corrode by other routes.

**Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.** Neither alone is enough. The oxygen in the air and the water must both be present, and the product is **hydrated iron(III) oxide** — the flaky orange-brown solid we call rust.

$$\text{iron} + \text{oxygen} + \text{water} \rightarrow \text{hydrated iron(III) oxide}$$

**Why rust is worse than other corrosion.** Rust **flakes off**, exposing fresh iron underneath, so the process continues until the whole object is destroyed. A coating that stayed in place would seal the surface — and that is exactly what aluminium does.

**Salt water speeds it up.** Dissolved salt makes the water a better conductor, so rusting is faster near the sea or on roads treated with grit, though salt is not *necessary* for rusting.

steps.title: Barrier methods
steps.body:
If rusting needs air and water, the simplest defence is to **keep them away from the iron**. **Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier.**

**Greasing**, **Painting**, **Electroplating** are the three the specification names.

- **Greasing** suits moving parts, such as a bicycle chain, where paint would be scraped off. It must be renewed.
- **Painting** suits large fixed structures — bridges, railings, ships — and is cheap over a wide area.
- **Electroplating** coats the iron with a thin layer of another metal using electrolysis, giving an even, durable finish.

**Aluminium is a special case.** It does not need a coating applied, because it **forms its own oxide coating** that **protects the metal from further corrosion**. Aluminium is actually **more reactive than iron**, so it reacts quickly with air — but the oxide layer that forms is **thin, tough and sticks tightly**, sealing the surface. Rust, by contrast, **flakes off**, which is why iron keeps corroding and aluminium does not.

**The weakness of every barrier** is that it only works while it is **complete**. A scratch in paint, or a gap in grease, lets air and water reach the iron and rusting begins there.

steps.title: Sacrificial protection
steps.body:
Some coatings do more than block air and water. **Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection.**

**How it works.** A metal **more reactive** than iron is attached to it or coated over it. Because it is more reactive, it **loses electrons more readily** and so **corrodes instead of the iron**. It is sacrificed to save the iron — hence the name.

**Galvanising.** **Zinc is used to galvanise iron**: the iron is coated with zinc. This works in **two** ways at once:

1. As a **barrier**, keeping air and water off the iron.
2. As **sacrificial protection**, because **zinc is more reactive than iron**, so even if the coating is scratched, the **zinc corrodes and the iron does not**.

That second point is the crucial difference from paint. A scratch in paint starts rusting; a scratch in galvanising does not.

**Choosing the metal.** It must be **above iron** in the reactivity series. **Zinc** and **magnesium** work; **tin** and **copper** do not, because they are **below** iron. Tin-plated steel — a "tin can" — is protected only while the tin is intact, and once scratched the iron actually rusts **faster**.

**Blocks of magnesium** are bolted to ships' hulls and underground pipelines for exactly this reason, and replaced when they have corroded away.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say both air and water, every time.** "Rusting needs oxygen" is half an answer. So is "rusting needs water". The specification says **both are necessary**, and the experiment is designed to prove exactly that.

**Explain what each tube removes.** Boiling removes **dissolved air**; the oil stops it redissolving; calcium chloride is a **drying agent** that removes **water vapour**. An answer that describes the tubes without saying what each is controlling has not explained the experiment.

**Distinguish barrier from sacrificial.** Paint, grease and electroplating are **barriers only**. Galvanising is **both**. That is why a scratched painted railing rusts and a scratched galvanised one does not — the single best discriminator in this topic.

**Justify sacrificial protection by reactivity.** Zinc and magnesium are **above** iron, so they corrode first. Tin is **below** iron, so a scratched tin can rusts **faster** than bare steel would. Naming the position in the series is what earns the mark.

**Explain aluminium properly.** It is **more reactive than iron**, and it does react — but its oxide layer is **tough and adheres**, sealing the surface, whereas **rust flakes off** and exposes fresh metal. The contrast is the answer.

**Account for the mass increase.** A rusting nail gets **heavier** because **oxygen from the air becomes part of the solid**. It is conservation of mass again, and questions link the two topics deliberately.

**Match the method to the situation.** Grease for moving parts, paint for large structures, galvanising where scratches are likely, magnesium blocks for ships and buried pipes. A recommendation without a reason drawn from the situation scores poorly.

**Salt speeds rusting but is not required.** Saying seawater is *necessary* is wrong; saying it **accelerates** rusting is right.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Corrosion** is the **destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment**.
- **Rusting** is corrosion of **iron and steel**.
- **Both air and water are necessary** for iron to rust.
- The product is **hydrated iron(III) oxide**, which **flakes off** and exposes fresh iron.
- **Three-tube experiment**: water and air → rusts; boiled water under oil → no rust; dry air with calcium chloride → no rust.
- **Barrier methods**: **greasing**, **painting**, **electroplating** — they keep air and water out.
- A barrier works only while it is **complete**.
- **Aluminium** forms an **oxide coating** that **protects the metal from further corrosion**, because the layer **adheres** rather than flaking.
- **Sacrificial protection** uses a **more reactive metal**, which **corrodes instead of** the iron.
- **Zinc galvanises iron** and acts as **both** a barrier and sacrificial protection.
- **Magnesium** blocks protect ships and pipelines.
- **Tin is below iron**, so tin plating protects only while intact.
- Rusting **increases** the mass of the iron, because oxygen joins it.
- **Salt** speeds rusting up but is **not necessary**.

questions.prompt:
A steel pier is to be built in a salt-water estuary and must last fifty years with minimal maintenance.

Explain why the steel would corrode rapidly in this location, and evaluate painting, galvanising and attaching magnesium blocks as ways of protecting it. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
Steel is mostly **iron**, and rusting requires **both air and water**. An estuary pier is permanently in contact with water and with the air above it, so both conditions are met continuously. The water is **salty**, and dissolved salt makes it a better conductor, which **speeds rusting up** considerably. The structure would therefore corrode far faster than the same steel inland.

**Painting** is a **barrier only**. It is cheap over a large area, but any **chip or scratch** — likely on a pier struck by boats and debris — exposes bare iron to salt water, and rusting then spreads beneath the paint as the rust flakes away. Over fifty years it would need repainting many times, which is exactly the maintenance to be avoided.

**Galvanising** coats the steel with **zinc**, and does two jobs. It is a **barrier**, and because **zinc is more reactive than iron** it also gives **sacrificial protection**: even where the coating is scratched, the **zinc corrodes in preference to the iron**. This is a decisive advantage in a location where damage to the coating is certain.

**Magnesium blocks** bolted to the structure work on the same principle and are even more strongly sacrificial, since magnesium is above zinc in the reactivity series. Their advantage is that they can be **inspected and replaced** without treating the whole structure; their drawback is that they **corrode away** and so must be renewed periodically.

For a fifty-year life with minimal maintenance, **galvanising the steel and fitting magnesium blocks** is the strongest combination: the zinc protects the whole surface including any scratches, while the blocks take the brunt of the attack and can be swapped out. Painting alone would not survive the conditions.

Rusting needs **both air and water** — say both. In the three-tube experiment, explain what each tube **removes**: boiling drives out dissolved air, oil keeps it out, and calcium chloride absorbs water vapour.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states that **both** air and water are necessary and explains the three-tube experiment by what each tube controls. It separates barrier from sacrificial protection and justifies the sacrificial metal by its position **above iron** in the reactivity series, using that to explain why a scratch defeats paint but not galvanising. It explains aluminium by the **adhering** oxide layer against flaking rust, accounts for the mass increase by oxygen joining the solid, notes that salt accelerates rather than causes rusting, and matches its recommendation to the situation described.
